abstract: Herbivorous insects that feed on toxic plants have not only evolved to tolerate the chemical defenses of their hosts, but to co-opt them for their own defenses. Previous research has shown that the tobacco hornworm (Manduca sexta), a specialist herbivore of alkaloid-rich Solanaceous plants, is capable of exhaling ingested nicotine to defend itself from spiders; a phenomenon known as defensive halitosis. In this study, we aimed to uncover the effect of nicotine on interactions between predatory lizards (Uta stansburiana) and lepidopteran larvae (Manduca sexta and Spodoptera exigua). We leveraged transgenic lines of wild tobacco (Nicotiana attenuata) that are unable to produce nicotine or that inhibit M. sextas defensive halitosis via RNAi. We found that ingested nicotine in prey altered the rates of chemosensory and aggressive behaviors performed by lizards, yet there was no effect of inhibiting M. sextas ability to use ingested nicotine in a defensive halitosis. Furthermore, we found that nicotine had no effect on interactions between lizards and S. exigua larvae. These results suggest that nicotine on the surface of tobacco-feeding insects, but not volatile nicotine, influences lizard behavior in a dose-dependent manner rather than being a universally aversive chemical cue.
